title: Valuation of a field norm over a finite semilocal DVR algebra
statement: Let $A$ be a discrete valuation ring [def-sc-discrete-valuation-ring] with fraction field $K$ and residue field $k$. Let $B$ be a commutative integral domain containing $A$ which is finite as an $A$-module [def-weil-finitely-generated-module], and let $L=\operatorname{Frac}(B)$ be a finite extension of $K$ [def-pc-field-extension, def-weil-vector-space-dimension] through this inclusion. Suppose that the set $X$ of maximal ideals of $B$ is finite, that every $\mathfrak q\in X$ contracts to the maximal ideal of $A$, that each $B_{\mathfrak q}$ [def-weil-pbc-localization-at-prime] is a discrete valuation ring, and that $f_{\mathfrak q}=[B/\mathfrak q:k]$ is finite. For any discrete valuation ring $R$ with fraction field $F$, write $v_R:F^\times\to\mathbf Z$ for its normalized valuation: $v_R(x)=r$ when $x=u t^r$ for a unit $u\in R^\times$ and a uniformizer $t$ of $R$, with $r\in\mathbf Z$. Define $N_{L/K}(y)$ to be the determinant [def-weil-endomorphism-determinant] over $K$ of the $K$-linear map $L\to L$, $z\mapsto yz$. Then for every $y\in L^\times$ one has $$v_A(N_{L/K}(y))=\sum_{\mathfrak q\in X}f_{\mathfrak q}\,v_{B_{\mathfrak q}}(y).$$

source.place: Tag 02MJ (lemma-finite-extension-dim-1), norm/order formula specialized to discrete valuation rings, with order expressed as normalized uniformizer exponent.

proof.text: Regard $B$ as an $A$-submodule of $L$ and let $S$ be its $K$-linear span. Finite $A$-generators [def-weil-finitely-generated-module] also span $S$ over $K$, so $S$ is finite-dimensional [def-weil-finite-dimensional-subspace]. It contains $1$, is closed under multiplication, and is contained in the field $L$. For a nonzero $c\in S$, multiplication by $c$ is an injective $K$-linear endomorphism of the finite-dimensional space $S$, hence is surjective; in particular $1=cz$ for some $z\in S$. Thus $S$ is a subfield containing $B$ and therefore contains its fraction field $L$. Consequently $S=L$, so $B$ is a finite $A$-submodule spanning $L$.

source.place: Tag 02MJ (lemma-finite-extension-dim-1), the lattice B in L used in the final proof paragraph; spanning verified explicitly.

proof.text: Fix $y\in L^\times$ and let $g:L\to L$ be multiplication by $y$, an invertible $K$-linear map with inverse multiplication by $y^{-1}$. Put $H=B\cap yB$ inside $L$, and $M_+=B/H$, $M_-=yB/H$. The intersection $H$ is a $B$-submodule of both $B$ and $yB$ because multiplication in $L$ is commutative. Apply [lem-exc-dvr-lattice-distance-determinant] to $R=A$, $V=L$, the lattice $B$ from Step 1 and $g$. It gives finite $A$-length of both $M_+$ and $M_-$, and $$v_A(N_{L/K}(y))=\ell_A(M_+)-\ell_A(M_-),$$ since $N_{L/K}(y)$ is by definition the determinant of multiplication by $y$ [def-weil-endomorphism-determinant].

source.place: Tags 02MI (lemma-order-vanishing-determinant) and 02MG (definition-distance), applied to the lattice B as in Tag 02MJ.

proof.text: Every strict chain of $B$-submodules of either $M_+$ or $M_-$ is also a strict chain of $A$-submodules. Thus the finite $A$-lengths in Step 2 imply finite $B$-lengths by [def-weil-pbc-module-length]. Apply [lem-exc-semilocal-restriction-length] separately to these two $B$-modules. The hypotheses hold: $X$ is finite, every maximal ideal contracts to $\mathfrak m_A$, and the residue degrees $f_{\mathfrak q}$ are finite by assumption. Subtract the resulting two finite sums, in $\mathbf Z$, to obtain $$v_A(N_{L/K}(y))=\sum_{\mathfrak q\in X}f_{\mathfrak q}\bigl(\ell_{B_{\mathfrak q}}((M_+)_{\mathfrak q})-\ell_{B_{\mathfrak q}}((M_-)_{\mathfrak q})\bigr).$$

source.place: Tag 02M0 (lemma-pushdown-module), applied to the two quotient modules in the distance formula of Tag 02MI.

proof.text: Fix $\mathfrak q\in X$ and put $R=B_{\mathfrak q}$ [def-weil-pbc-localization-at-prime]. Since $B$ is a domain, every denominator outside $\mathfrak q$ is nonzero, so these localizations embed in $L$. The localizations of $B$ and $yB$ inside $L$ are $R$ and $yR$. Also $\operatorname{Frac}(R)=L$: the inclusions $B\subseteq R\subseteq L$ show that $\operatorname{Frac}(R)\subseteq L$, and every fraction of elements of $B$ is a fraction of elements of $R$, giving the reverse inclusion. Moreover $H_{\mathfrak q}=R\cap yR$: if $x=b/s=yc/t$ with $b,c\in B$ and $s,t\notin\mathfrak q$, then $stx=tb=ysc\in B\cap yB=H$, so $x\in H_{\mathfrak q}$; the reverse inclusion is immediate. Apply [lem-weil-pbc-localization-module-exact] to the quotient exact sequences $H\to B\to M_+$ and $H\to yB\to M_-$. The localized quotient maps are surjective (lift a fraction of a quotient to the fraction of any representative) by [def-weil-pbc-module-localization]. Hence they induce $R$-linear isomorphisms $$(M_+)_{\mathfrak q}\cong R/(R\cap yR),\qquad (M_-)_{\mathfrak q}\cong yR/(R\cap yR).$$ Each isomorphism identifies submodules in both directions by image and inverse image and preserves strict inclusions; therefore the corresponding module lengths are equal by [def-weil-pbc-module-length].

source.place: Tags 02M0 and 02MI; identification of the localized quotients and intersection, written explicitly from fractions.

proof.text: The ring $R$ is a DVR by hypothesis and [def-sc-discrete-valuation-ring]. It is a principal ideal domain, so [lem-weil-pbc-pid-noetherian-normal] gives Noetherianity. Fix a uniformizer $t$. By [lem-weil-pbc-dvr-unit-times-uniformizer-power], each nonzero principal ideal of $R$ is $(t^j)$ for some $j\geq0$. Since every ideal is principal, the ideals containing $(t^n)$ are precisely $(t^j)$ for $0\leq j\leq n$; if $j>n$ and $t^n\in(t^j)$, cancellation would make the nonunit $t$ invertible, so necessarily $j\leq n$; divisibility of powers gives the reverse order on the exponents. Submodules of $R/(t^n)$ are the corresponding ideals modulo $(t^n)$, so their longest strict chain has length $n$, and $\ell_R(R/(t^n))=n$ by [def-weil-pbc-module-length], also for $n=0$. Every nonzero fraction $y=a/b$ with $a,b\in R$ has such a form: apply the cited power lemma to $a=u_1t^i$ and $b=u_2t^j$ to get $y=(u_1u_2^{-1})t^{i-j}$. The exponent is unique, since equality of two such forms with different exponents would make a positive power of $t$ a unit. Thus write $y=ut^r$ with $u\in R^\times$, $r=v_R(y)\in\mathbf Z$, using the normalized-valuation convention stated above. If $r\geq0$, then $yR=t^rR\subseteq R$ and the two lengths in Step 4 are $r$ and $0$. If $r=-n<0$, then $R\subseteq yR=t^{-n}R$ and the two lengths are $0$ and $n$: multiplication by $t^n$ identifies $yR/R$ with $R/t^nR$. In both cases the first length minus the second is $v_R(y)$.

source.place: Tag 02MD (definition-ord), normalized to the uniformizer exponent using Tag 00PD (lemma-characterize-dvr); the ideal-chain and negative-exponent calculations are written out.

proof.text: Substitute the local difference computed in Steps 4 and 5 into the sum in Step 3. This yields $$v_A(N_{L/K}(y))=\sum_{\mathfrak q\in X}f_{\mathfrak q}\,v_{B_{\mathfrak q}}(y).$$ The argument used only $y\ne0$ and includes units, positive valuations and negative valuations, so it proves the assertion for every $y\in L^\times$.
